lead: Four quantities decide antenna performance. Radiation resistance turns radiated power into an equivalent resistor. Efficiency says how much input power escapes instead of heating metal. Effective aperture says how much of an incoming wave is captured. Polarization decides whether the wave can be received at all. Together they set the power budget of every radio link, from FM to satellite.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the radiated field of a current element, and Chapter 2.2 for directivity and gain.

sections.h3: Radiation resistance: the resistor that is not there

blocks.text: Drive a dipole and it draws current as if a resistor sat at its terminals. That resistor does not exist: the power has left as a wave. It is the radiation resistance R<sub>r</sub>, defined so the radiated power comes out right:

blocks.where: P<sub>rad</sub> is total radiated power in W; I is peak current in A at a stated reference point; R<sub>r</sub> is in Ω. With rms current the ½ disappears.

blocks.text: I must be quoted at a stated point: terminals or current maximum. A folded dipole shows four times the input resistance of a plain dipole for the same radiated power, because its feed current splits between two paths.

Two short-dipole conventions. An infinitesimal dipole with the same current all along has R<sub>r</sub> = 80π²(l/λ)², referred to terminal current. A real short dipole has triangular current, zero at the tips; referred to the current maximum, R<sub>r</sub> = 20π²(l/λ)², one quarter as large. l is dipole length in m; λ is free-space wavelength in m.

A half-wave dipole has 73 Ω at its current maximum. A quarter-wave monopole over a ground plane has 36.5 Ω, half, because it fills half the sphere. On the triangular convention the short dipole falls fast: about 2 Ω at l = λ/10, and 0.08 Ω at λ/50.

Metal resistance and insulator leakage collect into one loss resistance R<sub>L</sub>, so input resistance is R<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>. Only R<sub>r</sub> radiates; R<sub>L</sub> heats.

blocks.where: η<sub>rad</sub> is radiation efficiency, a plain ratio; R<sub>r</sub> and R<sub>L</sub> are in Ω. A value of 0.8 means 80 per cent of accepted power leaves as radiation.

blocks.text: Gain and directivity are linked by G = η<sub>rad</sub> D, with D and G plain ratios; convert to dB afterwards. Loss does not change the pattern, so D is untouched while G drops.

Small antennas are hard because R<sub>r</sub> is small. Two ohms in series with 0.5 Ω of matching coil throws away 20 per cent. At l = λ/50 the same 0.5 Ω leaves η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.08/(0.08+0.5) ≈ 0.14, so most input power heats the metal. A half-wave dipole at 73 Ω sits far above typical loss and is naturally efficient.

On receive, an antenna behaves like a catching area. If the incoming wave carries power density S in W/m² and the antenna delivers P<sub>r</sub> watts to a matched load, effective aperture is A<sub>e</sub> = P<sub>r</sub>/S, in m².
A<sub>e</sub> = D λ² / (4π)   or   A<sub>e</sub> = G λ² / (4π) with loss
blocks.where: A<sub>e</sub> is effective aperture in m²; D is directivity and G is gain, both plain ratios; λ is free-space wavelength in m. The relation holds for any antenna shape.

blocks.text: A<sub>e</sub> is not physical area. A half-wave dipole at 300 MHz has D = 1.64 and A<sub>e</sub> = 1.64 × 1/(12.57) ≈ 0.13 m², though it is a thin half-metre wire. Only for D = 1 does A<sub>e</sub> equal λ²/4π.

For a real opening — horn mouth, dish — aperture efficiency e<sub>ap</sub> = A<sub>e</sub>/A<sub>phys</sub>. It stays below 1 because the field across the opening is not uniform and some power spills past the rim; 0.5 to 0.7 is usual for a dish.

sections.h3: Polarization and the polarization loss factor

blocks.text: Polarization is the path traced by the electric field tip as the wave passes, looking along travel. Linear: a fixed straight line. Circular: a circle, traced once per period. Elliptical: an ellipse, the general case. Axial ratio AR is major axis divided by minor axis: 1 for circular, infinite for linear.

Build circular polarization from two crossed dipoles fed equal currents with a 90° phase difference. The linear fields add in quadrature and the resultant rotates. Reverse the 90° and the sense flips between right-hand and left-hand circular; wrong sense on a satellite link throws the signal away.

When wave and antenna differ, only the component along the antenna is picked up. Unit vectors in the plane perpendicular to propagation: ρ̂<sub>w</sub> for the wave, ρ̂<sub>a</sub> for the antenna. The polarization loss factor multiplies received power:

blocks.where: ρ̂<sub>w</sub> and ρ̂<sub>a</sub> are unit vectors for wave and antenna polarization; PLF is a plain ratio between 0 and 1.

items: Matched polarizations: PLF = 1, that is 0 dB.
Linear antenna against a circular wave: PLF = 0.5, a 3 dB loss.
Crossed linear, vertical against horizontal: PLF = 0, a complete null.
Circular against circular of opposite sense: PLF = 0.

figure.caption: Below about λ/10 the radiation resistance grows as the square of electrical length; by λ/2 it has reached 73 Ω and the square law no longer holds. The quarter-wave monopole sits at exactly half the dipole value.

examples.question: A short dipole has length l = λ/20 and a loss resistance R<sub>L</sub> = 0.5 Ω. Find (a) its radiation resistance on the triangular-current convention, (b) its radiation efficiency, and (c) its effective aperture at 300 MHz, taking D = 1.5.
steps: Total resistance: R<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub> = 0.4935 + 0.5 = 0.9935 Ω ≈ 0.99 Ω.
Efficiency: η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.4935/0.9935 = 0.497 ≈ 0.50, that is 50 per cent.
Wavelength: λ = c/f = (3 × 10⁸ m/s)/(300 × 10⁶ Hz) = 1 m.
With loss charged to the aperture: A<sub>e</sub> = η<sub>rad</sub>Dλ²/(4π) = 0.497 × 0.119 = 0.059 m².
examples.answer: R<sub>r</sub> ≈ 0.49 Ω, η<sub>rad</sub> ≈ 0.50 (50 per cent), and A<sub>e</sub> ≈ 0.119 m² from D = 1.5, falling to 0.059 m² once the loss is included.
examples.check:
import math
lam_ratio = 1/20
Rr = 20*math.pi**2*lam_ratio**2
RL = 0.5
eta = Rr/(Rr+RL)
f = 300e6
c = 3e8
lam = c/f
D = 1.5
Ae = D*lam**2/(4*math.pi)
Ae_lossy = eta*Ae
print(round(Rr,2))
print(round(eta,2))
print(round(Ae,3))
print(round(Ae_lossy,3))

traps: Quoting R<sub>r</sub> without saying which current it refers to. A folded dipole has four times the input resistance of a plain dipole for the same radiated power; the number is meaningless without a reference point.
Using A<sub>e</sub> = λ²/4π for every antenna. That value belongs to D = 1 alone; multiply by D or G for anything else.
Mixing peak and rms current in P<sub>rad</sub> = ½|I|²R<sub>r</sub>. This halves or doubles computed R<sub>r</sub>; the efficiency error depends on R<sub>L</sub>.
Measuring radiation resistance with a multimeter. A DC ohmmeter sees only R<sub>L</sub>; R<sub>r</sub> exists only at the operating frequency and only as radiated power.
Forgetting the polarization loss factor, or calling axial ratio 1 a linear wave. AR = 1 is circular, AR → ∞ is linear, and linear against circular quietly costs 3 dB.

quiz.q: Define radiation resistance and state the condition attached to it.
quiz.a: R<sub>r</sub> is the equivalent resistance accounting for radiated power, defined by P<sub>rad</sub> = ½|I|²R<sub>r</sub>. I must be quoted at a stated reference point, usually terminals or current maximum.

quiz.q: State the radiation resistance of a half-wave dipole and of a quarter-wave monopole, and give the reason for the ratio.
quiz.a: 73 Ω for a half-wave dipole at its current maximum, and 36.5 Ω for a quarter-wave monopole over a ground plane. The monopole radiates into half the sphere, so for the same current it radiates half the power.

quiz.q: Why does a very short dipole have poor radiation efficiency even when its loss resistance is small?
quiz.a: R<sub>r</sub> falls as (l/λ)², becoming tiny — about 0.08 Ω at λ/50 on the triangular-current convention. Efficiency R<sub>r</sub>/(R<sub>r</sub>+R<sub>L</sub>) then has a small numerator, and even 0.5 Ω of coil or conductor loss dominates, sending most input power into heat.

quiz.q: An antenna has D = 20 and η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.9 at 3 GHz. Find its gain in dB and its effective aperture.
A vertical linear antenna receives a right-hand circular wave with power density S = 1 mW/m². The antenna's effective aperture is 0.02 m². Find the power delivered to a matched load.
quiz.a: Linear against circular gives PLF = |ρ̂<sub>w</sub> · ρ̂<sub>a</sub>|² = 0.5, a 3 dB loss. P<sub>r</sub> = S A<sub>e</sub> PLF = 1 × 10⁻³ × 0.02 × 0.5 = 1 × 10⁻⁵ W = 10 µW.

quiz.q: What does axial ratio describe, and what are its values for circular and linear polarization?
quiz.a: Axial ratio is the major axis of the polarization ellipse divided by the minor axis. AR = 1 means circular; AR tends to infinity means linear; anything between is elliptical.

quiz.q: Two crossed dipoles are fed with equal currents. What polarization results if the feed phase difference is 90°, and what happens if it is 0°?
quiz.a: At 90° the two orthogonal linear fields are in time quadrature with equal amplitude, so the resultant rotates: circular polarization, with sense set by the sign of the 90°. At 0° the fields add in phase and stay on one line at 45°, giving linear polarization with AR = ∞, not circular.

beyond: Not for the exam. In handsets and mmWave modules the small-antenna problem leads to the Chu limit and Wheeler's work on small antennas. Polarization matters in satellite and 5G links: dual-circular feeds, polarization diversity and MIMO rest on the PLF idea. Aperture efficiency is the quiet battleground of dish and horn design, since it directly buys decibels. Useful search terms: polarization diversity, axial ratio bandwidth, aperture efficiency of a reflector, gain comparison method in an antenna test range.
